Are we faced with too much choice?

‘Decision fatigue’ is the term that has been coined for the deteriorating quality of decisions made by an individual after a long session of decision making. Constant decision making can be overwhelming. Think about something as simple as grocery shopping after work. Do you get the organic berries at $7 or the non-organic at $4? Which style of pasta? Which brand of juice? It may seem liberating to live in a land of infinite choices, but research in decision making suggests otherwise.

In a study looking at choice and decision making, Stanford University researchers in the US set up a stall at an upmarket grocery store chosen for its ‘extraordinary selection’ of items for sale, including 300 types of jam. One Saturday afternoon, they loaded their stall with 24 jams; on the next Saturday, they did the same but with just six jams. They found that customers did seem to like the idea of having a lot of choices — more customers approached the 24-jam stall than the six-jam one — but people visiting the 24-jam booth tended to taste only one or two jams, the same number as in the six-jam group. When it came to buying jam, people faced with 24 jams were overwhelmed by the sheer number of choices they could make. Only 3 percent of the people at the 24-jam stall bought any jam, whereas 30 percent of people at the six-jam stall took home a jar of jam. The researchers called this behaviour ‘choice overload’ and recognised that choice overload leads to decision fatigue.

Still more research has found that repeated decision making also leads to some loss of self-control. Maintaining self-control takes subconscious thought and effort. For example, resisting the temptation to eat a cake readily available at work can mean that you are resisting a low-level distraction throughout the day. In the same way that a muscle gets tired from exertion, maintaining self-control in one area causes a short-term weakening in people's subsequent acts of self-control. Scientists have found that the mental effort of maintaining self-control has effects on even seemingly unrelated tasks, such as reducing a person's stamina when squeezing a handgrip and how long they work on solving a frustrating problem. Making decisions and exhibiting self-control are inescapable daily activities: getting overwhelmed and sometimes making bad, impulsive decisions are occupational hazards of being human.

There are some strategies that can be used to reduce decision fatigue. To begin with, get the important decisions out of the way early each morning before your concentration is interrupted by thoughts of lunch or after-work activities. Checking off your to-do list in an orderly manner when your mental resources are fresh is a good strategy for avoiding rash decisions. Next, decrease your range of options. This may seem counterintuitive, since it requires making even more decisions. For instance, if you're picking a restaurant for an important lunch meeting, beginning by deciding on a certain part of town or type of cuisine can narrow your options. Like the participants in the jams study, you're less likely to be paralysed by choice if you have only a few options instead of dozens.

Once you've arrived at a decision, stick with it and don't change your mind. This means that you have to ignore the voice in your head that is creating uncertainty. Just accept that no decision is ever perfect, and remind yourself that it is the best you can do with the tools you have at the moment you make the decision.

Another strategy people can consider when trying to reduce decision fatigue is to decide on a self-imposed maximum time for decision making. For example, when buying a new laptop bag, it is possible to spend a really long time studying the features of each bag, different prices and estimating value for money, but, by imposing a limit of only five minutes to make a decision, there are only so many bags that can be considered. This will save time, and research findings show that people are happier about the decisions they make too. For less important tasks that involve decision making, consider outsourcing them. For example, if you're wondering whether to go to the gym after work or call a client, let someone else make the decision for you. Always remember that after a time of decision making it is important to give yourself a break because productivity decreases over time, so go for a walk or take a long lunch so that you come back fresh.
